title: Capture your full employer 401(k) / 403(b) match
summary: Contribute exactly enough to get the entire employer match — not less, not more (yet).
detailsHtml:
The math

A typical match formula is "50% of contributions up to 6% of salary" or "100% on the first 3%, 50% on the next 2%." Either way, the match represents an immediate 50–100% return on the matched dollars. No risk-adjusted investment available to retail investors competes with this.

$60,000 salary, 50% match on first 6% = $60,000 × 6% = $3,600 employee contribution $3,600 × 50% = $1,800 employer match Immediate return: 50% (before any investment gains)

Why exactly the match — not more — at this stage

Above the match, the 401(k) competes with paying down high-interest debt and other priorities. Below the match, you're leaving free money on the table. The match is a discrete optimization point.

${bracketBlock( 'If your employer offers a Roth 401(k) option, strongly prefer it. Your current marginal rate is low enough that paying tax now and withdrawing tax-free in retirement is almost certainly the better deal.', 'Either Roth or Traditional 401(k) can be rational depending on whether you expect to be in a higher or lower bracket in retirement. Split contributions are a reasonable hedge. Note: employer match contributions were historically pre-tax only, but SECURE 2.0 §604 now permits (does not require) plans to offer Roth employer match — many large-plan recordkeepers added the option through 2025–26. If your match is Roth, it counts as taxable income in the year of contribution (reported on W-2 Box 12 with code AA/BB context per IRS guidance), and §604(a) requires the Roth-elected portion to be immediately 100% vested at contribution — plans with graded or cliff vesting cannot offer Roth match on the non-vested portion. The vesting requirement is the dominant plan-administration limit on §604 adoption to date.', 'Strongly prefer Traditional 401(k). The deduction is worth 32–37 cents on the dollar today, and most high earners drop one or more brackets in retirement. Pay tax later at the lower rate.' )}

Vesting

Check whether your match has a vesting schedule. Some employers vest immediately; others vest over 3–5 years. If your tenure is uncertain, the match's true value is the present value of the vested portion, not the headline number.

What your match is actually worth
